title: How does Kafka handle backpressure, and how does it affect consumer lag and throughput (pull model, manual offset, scaling consumers)?
shortTitle: How Kafka handles backpressure and its effect on lag and throughput

s1_definition.profdef: Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer signals that it cannot keep up, so the system slows the flow to it rather than overwhelming it. Kafka handles backpressure naturally through its pull-based model: consumers fetch records at their own pace, so a slow consumer simply polls less and fetches fewer records instead of being flooded by a push. The unprocessed records remain safely in the durable log, and the backlog shows up as consumer lag rather than lost data or memory pressure. You manage the effect by controlling fetch and poll sizes, committing offsets manually after real work, and scaling consumers up to the partition count to raise throughput.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's documents arriving in a big filing cabinet (the Kafka log). A push system would be a conveyor belt dumping documents onto a clerk's desk faster than the clerk can file them, burying the clerk. Kafka's pull model is different: the clerk walks to the cabinet and takes only as many documents as they can handle right now. If the clerk is slow, they just take fewer and the cabinet simply holds the rest safely. The growing pile in the cabinet waiting for that clerk is the lag. To go faster, you hire more clerks, up to the number of drawers, so they can file in parallel.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka's pull model gives backpressure for free, so a slow consumer fetches less and the backlog becomes durable lag rather than overload, and you raise throughput by tuning fetch sizes and scaling consumers up to the partition count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer signals that it cannot keep up, so the system slows the flow to it rather than overwhelming it. Kafka handles backpressure naturally through its pull-based model: consumers fetch records at their own pace, so a slow consumer simply polls less and fetches fewer records instead of being flooded by a push. The unprocessed records remain safely in the durable log, and the backlog shows up as consumer lag rather than lost data or memory pressure. You manage the effect by controlling fetch and poll sizes, committing offsets manually after real work, and scaling consumers up to the partition count to raise throughput.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's documents arriving in a big filing cabinet (the Kafka log). A push system would be a conveyor belt dumping documents onto a clerk's desk faster than the clerk can file them, burying the clerk. Kafka's pull model is different: the clerk walks to the cabinet and takes only as many documents as they can handle right now. If the clerk is slow, they just take fewer and the cabinet simply holds the rest safely. The growing pile in the cabinet waiting for that clerk is the lag. To go faster, you hire more clerks, up to the number of drawers, so they can file in parallel.

**One line to remember:** Kafka's pull model gives backpressure for free, so a slow consumer fetches less and the backlog becomes durable lag rather than overload, and you raise throughput by tuning fetch sizes and scaling consumers up to the partition count.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is the pull model. Unlike systems that push messages to consumers, Kafka consumers call `poll()` to request records. The broker never forces records onto a consumer, so a consumer that is busy simply does not poll as often or fetches fewer records per poll. This is inherent backpressure: the consumer controls its own intake rate. The records it has not fetched stay in the partition log, which is durable and bounded only by retention, so nothing is lost and the consumer's memory is not flooded. This is why Kafka is so robust under load compared to push-based queues that can overwhelm a consumer.

Several settings shape how much a consumer pulls. `max.poll.records` caps how many records one poll returns, which bounds the batch the consumer must process before the next poll. `fetch.min.bytes` and `fetch.max.wait.ms` let the broker wait to accumulate data for efficiency. Crucially, `max.poll.interval.ms` is the deadline by which the consumer must call poll again; if processing a batch takes longer than this, the broker assumes the consumer is dead and triggers a rebalance. So backpressure must be balanced: if a consumer pulls too large a batch and processing is slow, it can blow past the poll interval and get kicked out, which ironically makes things worse. The remedy is to pull smaller batches so each poll cycle finishes in time.

Manual offset management is central to safe backpressure. With auto-commit off, the consumer commits the offset only after it has actually finished processing a batch, so the committed position always reflects real completed work. This means that if the consumer is slow or restarts, it resumes exactly where real processing stopped, and the lag honestly reflects outstanding work. With auto-commit on, offsets can advance before processing finishes, which both risks data loss on a crash and makes lag understate the true backlog.

The effects on lag and throughput are direct. When a consumer is slower than production, its pull rate falls below the produce rate and lag grows; the lag is the visible, durable record of backpressure. Throughput for a consumer group is ultimately limited by partition count, because each partition is consumed by at most one consumer in a group. So to clear a backlog and raise throughput you add consumers up to the number of partitions, and beyond that you must add partitions. Other levers include making processing faster, batching downstream calls, and parallelizing work within a consumer carefully. The senior nuances are that pull-based backpressure converts overload into lag instead of failure, which buys you time to react; that you size `max.poll.records` to keep each poll cycle under the poll interval; that manual commit keeps lag honest and processing at-least-once; and that scaling consumers only helps up to the partition count, which is why partition count is a capacity-planning decision made early.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's settlement consumer calls a slow downstream risk engine, so it processes records more slowly than they are produced during market hours. In a push system it would be overwhelmed, but because Kafka is pull-based it simply fetches smaller batches and the backlog accumulates as durable lag. This is exactly how the pull model provides backpressure.

Problem 2 — The team initially set a huge max poll records, and processing a batch sometimes exceeded the poll interval, so the consumer was kicked out and rebalanced, making lag worse. They reduced the batch size so each poll cycle finished in time, and they switched to manual commit so offsets only advanced after real work. This is exactly how poll sizing and manual offsets manage backpressure.

Problem 3 — To clear the growing backlog they scaled consumers up to the partition count. This is exactly how scaling consumers raises throughput, bounded by partitions.

We simulate this in plain Java. A `Partition` holds produced records; a `PullConsumer` polls a bounded batch, processes at a given speed, and commits manually; a `ConsumerGroup` distributes partitions across consumers. The demo shows lag growing with one slow consumer, then shrinking when we scale to more consumers. The code will show: a `Partition`, a `PullConsumer`, a `ConsumerGroup`, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — backpressure-aware consumer tuning
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      enable-auto-commit: false          # manual commit AFTER processing
      max-poll-records: 100              # bound batch so poll cycle finishes in time
      properties:
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000     # deadline before broker evicts the consumer
        fetch.min.bytes: 1
        fetch.max.wait.ms: 500
    listener:
      ack-mode: MANUAL                   # commit explicitly
      concurrency: 12                    # up to partition count
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four partitions, each receiving one hundred records per tick, so four hundred produced per tick, consumed first by one slow consumer and then by four.

Step 1: In phase one, a single consumer owns all four partitions but can only process fifty records per poll on each partition. It pulls a bounded batch rather than being flooded, which is the pull model giving backpressure.

Step 2: Because production of four hundred per tick outpaces what the one consumer processes, the unprocessed records stay safely in the log and the total lag grows every tick. The lag is the durable, visible form of backpressure; nothing is lost and the consumer is not overwhelmed.

Step 3: The consumer commits only the records it actually processed, using manual commit, so the committed offset honestly reflects completed work and the lag number is truthful.

Step 4: In phase two the team scales to four consumers, matching the four partitions, so each partition now has its own consumer processing a full hundred per tick. Throughput rises to match or exceed production.

Step 5: With throughput now keeping pace, the backlog drains tick by tick and the total lag falls back toward zero. The demo shows that scaling consumers up to the partition count is what raised throughput, and that going beyond four consumers would not help because there are only four partitions.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producers ──400 rec/tick──→ Kafka log (durable, pull-based)
                                   │
                                   ▼  consumers PULL (poll), not pushed
  PHASE 1 (1 slow consumer, 50/tick/partition)
     fetch bounded by max.poll.records ─→ process slowly ─→ manual commit
     produce(400) > consume(≈200) ─→ backlog stays in log ─→ LAG GROWS ▲
                                                          (no overload, durable)
  PHASE 2 (4 consumers = 4 partitions)
     each partition has its own consumer ─→ throughput ↑ ─→ LAG DRAINS ▼
     adding a 5th consumer → idle (only 4 partitions) → no gain
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka handles backpressure almost for free because it is pull-based. Consumers call poll to fetch records at their own pace, so the broker never pushes records onto a consumer and a busy consumer simply polls less and fetches smaller batches instead of being flooded. The records it has not fetched stay in the durable partition log, bounded only by retention, so nothing is lost and the consumer's memory is never overwhelmed. That is the fundamental advantage over push-based queues, which can bury a slow consumer, and it is why Kafka stays stable under bursty load.

The visible effect of backpressure is consumer lag. When a consumer is slower than production, its pull rate falls below the produce rate and the backlog accumulates as lag. I think of lag as the honest, durable record of backpressure: it tells me the consumer is behind, but because the data is safely in the log, it buys me time to react rather than failing. To keep that signal truthful I use manual offset commits with auto-commit off, so the committed position only advances after real processing finishes, which also gives at-least-once semantics and means a restart resumes exactly where real work stopped.

Managing backpressure well comes down to a few levers. I bound intake with max poll records so each poll cycle finishes before the max poll interval deadline, because if processing a batch overruns that deadline the broker thinks the consumer is dead and triggers a rebalance, which makes things worse; the fix is smaller batches, not larger. To actually raise throughput and drain a backlog, I scale consumers, but only up to the partition count, because each partition is consumed by at most one consumer in a group, so a fifth consumer on a four-partition topic just sits idle. Beyond that I add partitions, make processing faster, or batch the downstream calls.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the settlement consumer calls a slow risk engine, so during market hours it falls behind and the backlog shows up as growing lag rather than an overloaded service, exactly because Kafka is pull-based. We first made the mistake of setting a huge poll batch that overran the poll interval and caused rebalances, so we reduced max poll records and switched to manual commit to keep lag honest. When the backlog grew, we scaled the consumer group up to the partition count and the lag drained. The senior framing I give is that Kafka turns overload into durable lag instead of failure, which is a gift, and that handling backpressure is really about tuning poll size to stay under the poll interval, committing manually so lag is truthful, and scaling consumers up to the partition count, with partition count itself being a capacity decision you must make early.

---

keyPoints: Consumer lag: monitor with kafka-consumer-groups.sh or Burrow
Under-replicated partitions: broker down or slow disk
Rebalancing storms: frequent consumer restarts or slow processing
